hook.line: Listen to the café on a busy morning and half the words seem to end in *-ico* or *-ito*. Nobody is asking for a tiny coffee. They're being friendly.
hook.en: Could I have a coffee, please? (to a waiter, formal)

examples.en: Do you want a bit of cake? (to a friend)

examples.es: Mi abuelita guardaba todas las tarjetas.
examples.en: My grandma kept all the cards.
I brought you a little present. (to a friend)

rule:
Add *-ito* or *-ita* to a word and it gets smaller, softer or friendlier: *regalo*, *regalito*; *abuela*, *abuelita*; *poco*, *poquito*.

In Colombia, when the word ends in *-to* or *-ta*, the ending is *-ico*: *momento*, *momentico*; *rato*, *ratico*; *tinto*, *tintico*; *gato*, *gatico*.

It keeps the word's *-o* or *-a*: *una casita*, *un gatico*, *las velitas*.

Mostly it's about warmth, not size. *¿Me regala un tintico?* is a polite, friendly way to order a normal coffee. *Un momentico* is a moment, said kindly. *Ahorita* means in a bit, and in Colombia that bit can be long.

English does this only now and then (doggy, little bit). Spanish does it all day.
smallPrint: Teachers call these diminutives (*diminutivos*). Spelling follows the sound: *poco* becomes *poquito*, so the hard *k* sound stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tintito* or *tintico* and type the whole line: *¿Me regala un ___?*
yourTurn.why: *Tinto* ends in *-to*, so in Colombia it's *-ico*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *casito* or *casita* and type the whole sentence: *Es una ___.*
yourTurn.why: *Casa* is an *-a* word, and the ending keeps it: *casita*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it the Colombian way, to a friend: Wait a sec. (use *momento*)
Type in Spanish: I brought you a little present. (to a friend)
Type in Spanish: I'm coming in a minute. (use *ahora*)
yourTurn.why: *Ahorita* is the friendly, Colombian in a bit.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it softer: *¿Quieres un poco de torta?*
yourTurn.why: *Poco* becomes *poquito*: the *c* turns to *qu* to keep its sound.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it warmer: *Mi abuela guardaba todas las tarjetas.*
yourTurn.answer: Mi abuelita guardaba todas las tarjetas.
yourTurn.why: *Abuelita* is how most people talk about a grandmother they loved.

pitfalls.why: People will understand you, but in Colombia a word ending in *-to* takes *-ico*.
Drop the last vowel first, and keep the *k* sound with *qu*: *poquito*.
The ending follows the word: *casa* is an *-a* word, so *-ita*.

personal: Order something at your favourite café the Colombian way, with one *-ico* or *-ito* (*¿Me regala un...?*).
